Mumbai and New Delhi each have three sites, Agra and Jaipur have two.

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) designates [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") of outstanding universal value to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") which have been nominated by countries which are signatories to the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-convention-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.[[2]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-2) <India> accepted the convention on 14 November 1977, making its sites eligible for inclusion on the list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-India-3)

As of 2023, there are 42 [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") located in <India>. Out of these, 34 are cultural, 7 are natural, and one, the [Khangchendzonga National Park](Khangchendzonga_National_Park "Khangchendzonga National Park"), is of mixed type. India has the [sixth largest](World_Heritage_Sites_by_country "World Heritage Sites by country") number of sites in the world. The first sites to be listed were the [Ajanta Caves](Ajanta_Caves "Ajanta Caves"), [Ellora Caves](Ellora_Caves "Ellora Caves"), [Agra Fort](Agra_Fort "Agra Fort"), and [Taj Mahal](Taj_Mahal "Taj Mahal"), all of which were inscribed in the 1983 session of the [World Heritage Committee](World_Heritage_Committee "World Heritage Committee"). The most recent site listed was [[4]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-4). At different times, two sites were listed as [endangered](List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger "List of World Heritage in Danger"): the [Manas Wildlife Sanctuary](Manas_National_Park "Manas National Park") was listed between 1992 and 2011 due to poaching and activities of the [Bodo](Boro_people "Boro people") militias,[[5]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-Manas-5) and the monuments at <Hampi> were listed between 1999 and 2006 due to risks from increased traffic and new constructions in surroundings.[[6]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-Hampi-6) One site is transnational, [The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier](The_Architectural_Work_of_Le_Corbusier "The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier") is shared with six other countries.[[7]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-Corbusier-7) In addition, India has 50 sites on its tentative list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-India-3)

**The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement** is a [World Heritage Site](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") consisting of a selection of 17 building projects in several countries by the Franco-Swiss architect [Le Corbusier](Le_Corbusier "Le Corbusier").[[1]](The_Architectural_Work_of_Le_Corbusier#cite_note-1) These sites demonstrate how [Modern Movement architecture](Modernism "Modernism") was applied to respond to the needs of society and show the global range of a style and an architect.[[2]](The_Architectural_Work_of_Le_Corbusier#cite_note-whs-2)

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) designates [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") of outstanding universal value to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") which have been nominated by countries which are signatories to the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-convention-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). content:
Based on my search of Wikipedia for "The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier" UNESCO World Heritage Site, I can confirm that **YES, India is one of the countries involved**. Here are the key details:

## Site Inscription Details

**Official Name:** The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement

**Reference Number:** 1321rev

**Inscription Year:** 2016 (40th Session)

**Criteria:** Cultural (i)(ii)(vi)

## Participating Countries and Sites

This World Heritage Site consists of **17 building projects across 7 countries** on three continents. The countries involved are:

1. **France** (10 sites) - Various locations including Paris, Poissy, Marseille, Pessac, Ronchamp, Saint-Dié-des-Vosges, Éveux, Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, and Firminy

2. **Switzerland** (2 sites) - Corseaux and Genève

3. **Germany** (1 site) - Stuttgart

4. **Belgium** (1 site) - Antwerp

5. **Argentina** (1 site) - La Plata

6. **Japan** (1 site) - Tokyo

7. **India** (1 site) - Chandigarh

## Indian Site Details

**Site Name:** Complexe du Capitole (Chandigarh Capitol Complex)

**Site ID:** 1321-014

**Location:** Chandigarh, India

**Coordinates:** 30°45′27″N 76°48′20″E

**Property Area:** 66 ha (160 acres)

**Buffer Zone:** 195 ha (480 acres)

The Chandigarh Capitol Complex includes several buildings designed by Le Corbusier:
- Palace of Assembly
- Secretariat Building
- Punjab and Haryana High Court
- Open Hand Monument

This was a significant cross-border nomination, making it one of the most international World Heritage Sites. The site demonstrates how Modern Movement architecture was applied to respond to the needs of society and shows the global range of Le Corbusier's architectural work.

Based on my research, I can provide you with comprehensive information about the Silk Roads UNESCO World Heritage sites and India's participation.

## Current UNESCO Silk Roads World Heritage Sites

There are currently **two** inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Sites related to the Silk Roads:

### 1. Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor
- **Inscription Date:** June 22, 2014 (38th Session)
- **Countries Involved:** China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan (3 countries)
- **Sites:** 33 locations
- **Length:** 5,000 km stretch from Central China to the Zhetysu region of Central Asia

### 2. Silk Roads: Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor
- **Inscription Date:** September 17, 2023 (45th Session)
- **Countries Involved:** Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan (3 countries)
- **Sites:** 31 locations
- **Length:** 886 km stretch in Central Asia

## India's Participation

**India is NOT currently part of any inscribed UNESCO Silk Roads World Heritage site.** However:

- India has **12 Silk Road sites on the tentative list** of UNESCO World Heritage Sites
- These sites are spread across **7 states**: Bihar, Jammu and Kashmir, Maharashtra, Puducherry, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, and Uttar Pradesh
- These sites have **not yet been inscribed** as part of a transnational Silk Roads UNESCO World Heritage nomination

## UNESCO Silk Roads Project Background

- **Initiated:** 1988 by UNESCO
- **Purpose:** To promote understanding of cultural diffusion across Eurasia and protection of cultural heritage
- **Approach:** The project has been implemented through multiple corridor nominations from different regions

## Summary

While India was historically an important part of the ancient Silk Road network (including the Maritime Silk Road), it has not yet participated in the transnational UNESCO World Heritage Silk Roads inscriptions to date. India's 12 Silk Road sites remain on the tentative list, awaiting potential future nomination as part of a larger transnational Silk Roads World Heritage nomination involving multiple countries.

Based on my research of the Wikipedia articles, here are the findings on UNESCO transnational/shared World Heritage Sites involving India:

## Transnational World Heritage Sites Involving India

### 1. **The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement**
- **Inscription Year:** 2016 (40th Session of the World Heritage Committee)
- **Partner Countries:** **7 countries** total
  - Argentina
  - Belgium
  - France
  - Germany
  - Switzerland
  - **India**
  - Japan
- **India's Component:** **Chandigarh Capitol Complex** located in Chandigarh (Union Territory)
- **UNESCO Reference:** 1321rev
- **Criteria:** Cultural (i), (ii), (vi)
- **Description:** This is a transnational site encompassing 17 building projects across three continents by the Franco-Swiss architect Le Corbusier. The Chandigarh Capitol Complex is the central part of the city of Chandigarh, designed in line with the principles of a "radiant city" (Ville Radieuse).

---

## Transboundary Ecosystem (Separate Inscriptions)

### 2. **The Sundarbans**
While not inscribed as a single shared site, the Sundarbans represents a transboundary ecosystem managed as **separate World Heritage Sites** in each country:

| Country | Site Name | Year Inscribed | UNESCO Reference |
|---------|-----------|----------------|------------------|
| **India** | Sundarbans National Park | 1987 | 452 |
| **Bangladesh** | The Sundarbans | 1997 | 798 |

- **Description:** The Sundarbans is the world's largest mangrove forest in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers. It spans both India (West Bengal) and Bangladesh.
- **India's Share:** 34% of the total Sundarbans area
- **Bangladesh's Share:** 66% of the total Sundarbans area
- **Criteria:** Natural (ix), (x)

---

## Summary

| Type of Site | Name | Partner Countries | Year (India) |
|--------------|------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Transnational** | The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier | Argentina, Belgium, France, Germany, India, Japan, Switzerland | 2016 |
| **Transboundary (separate inscriptions)** | Sundarbans | India, Bangladesh | India: 1987, Bangladesh: 1997 |

**Note:** As of 2023, India has **42 World Heritage Sites** total (34 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed). Only **one** is a true transnational site (Le Corbusier), while the Sundarbans represents a shared ecosystem with separate inscriptions in each country.

# Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

## Writing Instructions

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) designates [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") of outstanding universal value to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") which have been nominated by countries which are signatories to the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-convention-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.[[2]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-2) <India> accepted the convention on 14 November 1977, making its sites eligible for inclusion on the list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-India-3)

As of 2023, there are 42 [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") located in <India>. Location of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Mongolia. Red dots represent cultural and green dots represent natural sites.

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) designates [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") of outstanding universal value to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") which have been nominated by countries which are signatories to the UNESCO [World Heritage Convention](World_Heritage_Convention "World Heritage Convention"), established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Mongolia#cite_note-convention-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.[[2]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Mongolia#cite_note-2) <Mongolia> ratified the convention on 2 February 1990.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Mongolia#cite_note-Mongolia-3)

Mongolia has five sites on the list. The first site, the [Uvs Nuur Basin](Uvs_Nuur_Basin "Uvs Nuur Basin"), was listed in 2003. The most recent site, the Landscapes of Dauria, was listed in 2017. These two sites are natural and transnational sites; they are shared with Russia. The other three sites are cultural. In addition, Mongolia has 12 sites on the tentative list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Mongolia#cite_note-Mongolia-3)

## World Heritage Sites

UNESCO lists sites under [ten criteria](World_Heritage_Site#Selection_criteria "World Heritage Site"); each entry must meet at least one of the criteria. Criteria i through vi are cultural, and vii through x are natural.[[4]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Mongolia#cite_note-4)

- **Uvs Nuur Basin**: Transboundary site between Russia and Mongolia (No India involvement)
- **Landscapes of Dauria**: Transboundary site between Russia and Mongolia (No India involvement)

It appears that based on my searches, India does NOT currently have any transnational/transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites that are officially inscribed as shared with other countries. Let me verify this by searching more comprehensively.

Based on my comprehensive research across Wikipedia, I can now provide a complete answer about transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites and India's involvement.

## Key Findings

**India does NOT currently have any officially inscribed transboundary/transnational UNESCO World Heritage Sites as a partner country.**

However, I found several related transboundary sites in the Asian region and potential/considered sites involving India:

### Transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the Region (NOT including India)

**1. Uvs Nuur Basin (Uvs Lake Basin)**
- **Countries**: Russia and Mongolia
- **Year Inscribed**: 2003 (27th Session)
- **Type**: Natural
- **Criteria**: (ix)(x)
- **Reference No.**: 769rev
- **Area**: 8,980.635 km²
- **Description**: This site is an endorheic basin on the territorial border of Mongolia and Tuva (Russian Federation). It includes both the Russian component (Ubsunorskaya Kotlovina, designated 1997) and Mongolian component (Uvs Nuur Basin, designated 1997).

**2. Landscapes of Dauria**
- **Countries**: Russia and Mongolia
- **Year Inscribed**: 2017 (41st Session)
- **Type**: Natural
- **Criteria**: (ix)(x)
- **Reference No.**: 1448
- **Description**: This site encompasses the Daurian steppe and wetland ecosystem. It includes the Mongol Daguur Biosphere Reserve (Mongolia, designated 2005), Mongol Daguur (Strictly Protected Area), and Daursky Nature Reserve (Russia). A transboundary ecoregion straddling multiple countries.

### Silk Road Inscription (India NOT a partner)

**3. Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor**
- **Countries**: China, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan (India is NOT included)
- **Year Inscribed**: 2014 (38th Session)
- **Type**: Cultural
- **Reference No.**: 1442
- **Note**: India has **12 Silk Road sites on its tentative list** spread across seven states (Bihar, Jammu and Kashmir, Maharashtra, Puducherry, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, and Uttar Pradesh), but India is not part of this joint transnational inscription.

### India's World Heritage Sites with Potential Transboundary Connections

**4. Khangchendzonga National Park**
- **Location**: Sikkim, India
- **Year Inscribed**: 2016 (40th Session)
- **Type**: Mixed (cultural and natural)
- **Reference No.**: 1513
- **Note**: While Mount Kangchenjunga straddles the India-Nepal border (with 3 of 5 peaks directly on the border), this inscription is only for India's territory. Nepal also has a separate tentatively listed site on its side.

**5. Manas National Park**
- **Location**: Assam, India
- **Year Inscribed**: 1985 (removed from Danger List 2011)
- **Type**: Natural
- **Reference No.**: 338
- **Note**: borders Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan. While ecologically connected, these are **separate inscriptions**. Royal Manas is on Bhutan's tentative list but has not been jointly inscribed with India.

## Summary

**Conclusion**: Despite extensive searching, there are **no transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites where India is an official partner country**. While India shares natural features (mountains, rivers, ecosystems) with neighboring countries like Nepal, Bhutan, and Bangladesh, and has sites on its tentative list (including the Silk Road sites), no official transnational World Heritage inscription includes India as a signatory alongside other countries.

This is notable given India has 42 total World Heritage Sites (34 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed) and shares borders with 7 countries (Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Afghanistan).

content:
Based on my Wikipedia searches, I've found several important transboundary and border region heritage sites involving India and its neighbors. Here's a comprehensive summary:

## **Transboundary UNESCO Heritage Sites Involving India**

### **1. Manas National Park (India) - Bhutan Border**
- **Location:** Assam, northeastern India
- **UNESCO Status:** Natural World Heritage Site (designated 1985)
- **Transboundary Connection:** Borders **Royal Manas National Park** in Bhutan
- **Details:** This is one of the most significant transboundary protected areas involving India. The park was on the UNESCO "World Heritage in Danger" list from 1992-2011 due to poaching and security issues but was removed after conservation efforts. The Manas River itself is a transboundary river flowing through Bhutan, India, and China.

### **2. Khangchendzonga National Park (India) - Nepal Border**
- **Location:** Sikkim, India
- **UNESCO Status:** **Mixed Heritage Site** (cultural AND natural, designated 2016) - India's first mixed heritage site
- **Transboundary Connection:** Located on the **border with Nepal**, sharing Kangchenjunga mountain region
- **Details:** The sacred mountain Kangchenjunga straddles the Nepal-India border, with three of its five peaks directly on the border. This represents important transboundary cultural and natural heritage.

### **3. Kangchenjunga Conservation Area**
- **Transboundary Significance:** The Kangchenjunga region is shared between Nepal and India (Sikkim), representing one of the world's highest mountain regions with UNESCO recognition through Khangchendzonga National Park on the Indian side.

## **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Heritage Sites (Pakistan)**

### **Notable UNESCO Sites:**
- **Takht-i-Bahi and Sahr-i-Bahlol:** Buddhist monastery ruins from the 1st century CE, inscribed as World Heritage Site in 1980 - this is **the only complete UNESCO World Heritage Site** in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province
- **Other Heritage Sites:** Ranigat (Buddhist archaeological site, tentative listing), Mansehra Rock Edicts (Ashoka's edicts, tentative listing)

## **Great Himalayan National Park**
- **Location:** Himachal Pradesh, India
- **UNESCO Status:** Natural World Heritage Site (2014)
- **Note:** While a significant Himalayan conservation area, it is **NOT a transboundary site** - it's entirely within India

## **Shared Parks/Sites by Country**

### **India-Nepal:**
- No formal transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Site, but Khangchendzonga represents shared cultural significance
- Transboundary rivers include the Koshi/Kosi River flowing through China, Nepal, and India

### **India-Bhutan:**
- **Manas National Park** is the primary transboundary connection (continues as Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan)
- Both countries participate in the **Kangchenjunga** landscape-scale conservation

### **India-Bangladesh:**
- No transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites found, but the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta region is a major transboundary watershed

### **India-Myanmar:**
- No formal transboundary UNESCO sites identified in search results
- Shared border regions in northeastern India

### **India-Pakistan:**
- **No transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites** between India and Pakistan
- Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has significant cultural sites (Takht-i-Bahi) but these are on Pakistan's side only

## **Key Observations:**

1. **Most significant transboundary connection:** Manas National Park (India) ↔ Royal Manas National Park (Bhutan)
2. **Himalayan shared heritage:** Khangchendzonga represents India-Nepal border region cultural significance
3. **Regional cooperation:** The **International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD)** coordinates conservation across all eight Hindu Kush Himalaya countries (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan)

The search reveals that while there are border-sharing protected areas and significant heritage sites in border regions, **formal transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites involving India are relatively rare**, with the Manas-Royal Manas connection being the most prominent example.

Location of World Heritage Sites in Nepal

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) designates [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") of outstanding universal value to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") which have been nominated by countries which are signatories to the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Nepal#cite_note-convention2-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.[[2]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Nepal#cite_note-2) <Nepal> ratified the convention on 20 June 1978, making its historical sites eligible for inclusion on the list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Nepal#cite_note-main-3)

Four sites in Nepal were on the list in 2023, with a further fifteen on the tentative list, of sites that may be considered for future submission.[[4]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Nepal#cite_note-4) The first sites in Nepal to be added to the list were the [Sagarmatha National Park](Sagarmatha_National_Park "Sagarmatha National Park") and the [Kathmandu Valley](Kathmandu_Valley "Kathmandu Valley"), added in 1979. Due to the partial or substantial loss of the traditional elements of six out of seven monument zones and resulting general loss of authenticity and integrity of the whole property, Kathmandu Valley was also added to the [List of World Heritage in Danger](List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger "List of World Heritage in Danger") between 2003 and 2007. [Chitwan National Park](Chitwan_National_Park "Chitwan National Park") was listed in 1984, and <Lumbini>, the birthplace of Buddha according to Buddhist tradition, was added in 1997. The National Parks are natural sites, and the other two are cultural.

## World Heritage Sites

UNESCO lists sites under [ten criteria](World_Heritage_Site#Selection_criteria "World Heritage Site"); each entry must meet at least one of the criteria. Criteria i through vi are cultural, and vii through x are natural.[[5]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Nepal#cite_note-5)

The **Sacred Himalayan Landscape** is a 39,021 km2 (15,066 sq mi) large trans-boundary landscape in the eastern <Himalayas> encompassing [temperate broadleaf](Temperate_broadleaf_and_mixed_forest "Temperate broadleaf and mixed forest") and [conifer forests](Conifer_forest "Conifer forest"), alpine meadows and grasslands, which harbour more than 80 [mammal](Mammal "Mammal") and more than 440 [bird](Bird "Bird") [species](Species "Species"). It extends from <Nepal>'s [Langtang National Park](Langtang_National_Park "Langtang National Park") through <Sikkim> and <Darjeeling> in <India> to western <Bhutan>'s [Torsa Strict Nature Reserve](Torsa_Strict_Nature_Reserve "Torsa Strict Nature Reserve"). More than 73% of this landscape is located in Nepal, including [Sagarmatha National Park](Sagarmatha_National_Park "Sagarmatha National Park"), [Makalu Barun National Park](Makalu_Barun_National_Park "Makalu Barun National Park"), and [Kanchenjunga Conservation Area](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area "Kanchenjunga Conservation Area"). About 24% is located in India, encompassing [Khangchendzonga](Khangchendzonga_National_Park "Khangchendzonga National Park"), [Singalila](Singalila_National_Park "Singalila National Park") and [Neora Valley National Parks](Neora_Valley_National_Park "Neora Valley National Park") as well as [Fambong Lho](Fambong_Lho_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Fambong Lho Wildlife Sanctuary"), [Maenam](Maenam_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary"), [Senchal](Senchal_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary"), [Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuaries](Mahananda_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary"), [Shingba](Shingba_Rhododendron_Sanctuary "Shingba Rhododendron Sanctuary") and Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuaries and [Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary](Kyongnosla_Alpine_Sanctuary "Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary").[[1]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-Gurung_al2006-1)

It links the [Qomolangma National Nature Preserve](Qomolangma_National_Nature_Preserve "Qomolangma National Nature Preserve") in <Tibet>, one of the largest protected areas in Asia, with the [Kangchenjunga Landscape](Kangchenjunga#Protected_areas "Kangchenjunga") in India and the Bhutan Biological Conservation Complex in Bhutan.[[2]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-dnpwc-2)

[Climate change](Climate_change "Climate change") threatens the flora and fauna of this area. Trans-boundary protection of its biological and ecological connections is critical for the survival of such species as the [snow leopard](Snow_leopard "Snow leopard") and the [red panda](Red_panda "Red panda") that are threatened throughout the world.[[3]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-usaid-3)

## Sustainable livelihoods for the people

The area covers nine and a half million acres and includes five million people of diverse cultures who speak 40 languages.[[4]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-ww-shl-pdf-4) Most face abject poverty[[2]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-dnpwc-2) and are in need of [sustainable](Sustainable "Sustainable") livelihoods.[[4]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-ww-shl-pdf-4)

SHL is part of the initiation of the [World Wildlife Federation](World_Wide_Fund_for_Nature "World Wide Fund for Nature") (WWF) that "taps into the spiritual beliefs and conservation ethics of local communities to restore essential habitats and protect endangered species such as the [snow leopard](Snow_leopard "Snow leopard")."[[5]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-wwf-shl-5)

WWF has cooperated with the three governments of Nepal, India and Bhutan to preserve the fragile "complex mosaic of [biodiversity](Biodiversity "Biodiversity")" and "achieve conservation while creating
sustainable livelihoods in the Sacred Himalayan Landscape".[[4]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-ww-shl-pdf-4) The mountains in the SHL contain the future water supply, in the form of [glaciers](Glacier "Glacier"), for the huge population on the [Indian subcontinent](Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent") but are susceptible to natural disasters such as landslides, forest fires and flash floods that are caused by poor land management.[[4]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-ww-shl-pdf-4)

[The Mountain Institute](The_Mountain_Institute "The Mountain Institute") (TMI) has worked with farmers in the SHL by teaching them to cultivate medical plants, having trained over 12,500 since 2001.[[6]](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape#cite_note-6)

**Sagarmāthā National Park** is a [national park](National_park "National park") in the <Himalayas> of eastern <Nepal> that is dominated by [Mount Everest](Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"). It encompasses an area of 1,148 km2 (443 sq mi) in the [Solukhumbu District](Solukhumbu_District "Solukhumbu District") and ranges in elevation from 2,845 to 8,848 m (9,334 to 29,029 ft) at the summit of Mount Everest. In the north, it shares the international border with [Qomolangma National Nature Preserve](Qomolangma_National_Nature_Preserve "Qomolangma National Nature Preserve") in [Tibet Autonomous Region](Tibet_Autonomous_Region "Tibet Autonomous Region"). In the east, it is adjacent to [Makalu Barun National Park](Makalu_Barun_National_Park "Makalu Barun National Park"), and in the south it extends to [Dudh Kosi](Dudh_Kosi "Dudh Kosi") river.[[1]](Sagarmatha_National_Park#cite_note-nbrb2007-1) It is part of the [Sacred Himalayan Landscape](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape "Sacred Himalayan Landscape").[[2]](Sagarmatha_National_Park#cite_note-2)

## History

Sagarmatha National Park was established in 1976. In 1979, it became the country's first national park that was inscribed as a Natural [World Heritage Site](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"). In January 2002, a Buffer Zone comprising 275 km2 (106 sq mi) was added.[[1]](Sagarmatha_National_Park#cite_note-nbrb2007-1) Conservation of forests, wildlife, and cultural resources received top priority under the *Buffer Zone Management Guidelines*, followed by conservation of other natural resources and development of [alternative energy](Alternative_energy "Alternative energy").[[3]](Sagarmatha_National_Park#cite_note-3) Tourism in the area began in the early 1960s. In 2003, about 19,000 tourists arrived. As of 2005, about 3,500 [Sherpa people](Sherpa_people "Sherpa people") lived in villages and seasonal settlements situated along the main tourist trails.[[4]](Sagarmatha_National_Park#cite_note-4)

## Landscape

Sagarmatha National Park contains the upper [catchment](Catchment "Catchment") areas of the Dudh Kosi and Bhotekoshi rivers and the [Gokyo Lakes](Gokyo_Lakes "Gokyo Lakes"). It ranges in elevation from 2,845 m (9,334 ft) at Monjo to the top of [Mount Everest](Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") at 8,848 m (29,029 ft). Other peaks above 6,000 m (20,000 ft) are <Lhotse>, [Cho Oyu](Cho_Oyu "Cho Oyu"), <Thamserku>, <Nuptse>, <Amadablam> and <Pumori>. Barren land above 5,000 m (16,000 ft) comprises 69% of the park while 28% is grazing land and the remaining 3% is [forested](Forest "Forest"). Climatic zones span from [temperate](Montane_ecology "Montane ecology") and [subalpine](Montane_ecology "Montane ecology") above 3,000 m (9,800 ft) to [alpine](Alpine_tundra "Alpine tundra") above 4,000 m (13,000 ft), which is the upper limit of vegetation growth. The [nival](Snow "Snow") zone begins at 5,000 m (16,000 ft).[[1]](Sagarmatha_National_Park#cite_note-nbrb2007-1)

**Kanchenjunga Conservation Area** is a [protected area](Protected_area "Protected area") in the <Himalayas> of eastern <Nepal> that was established in 1997. It covers 2,035 km2 (786 sq mi) in the [Taplejung District](Taplejung_District "Taplejung District") and comprises two peaks of <Kanchenjunga>. In the north it adjoins the [Qomolangma National Nature Preserve](Qomolangma_National_Nature_Preserve "Qomolangma National Nature Preserve") in <Tibet>, and in the east the [Khangchendzonga National Park](Khangchendzonga_National_Park "Khangchendzonga National Park") in <Sikkim>.[[1]](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area#cite_note-nbrb2007-1) To the west it borders the [Sankhuwasabha District](Sankhuwasabha_District "Sankhuwasabha District"). It ranges in elevation from 1,200 to 8,586 m (3,937 to 28,169 ft). It is part of the [Sacred Himalayan Landscape](Sacred_Himalayan_Landscape "Sacred Himalayan Landscape"), which is being developed by [WWF](World_Wide_Fund_for_Nature "World Wide Fund for Nature") Nepal in partnership with the [International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development](International_Centre_for_Integrated_Mountain_Development "International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development").[[2]](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area#cite_note-aryal2010-2)

## History

When the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area was designated in March 1997, it was Nepal's third Conservation Area. In April 2003, a *Kanchenjunga Conservation Area Management Council* was formed with the support of WWF Nepal, comprising seven *Conservation Area User Committees*, 44 *User Groups*, and 32 *Mother Groups*. These community based institutions support effective implementation of all planned activities. In August 2006, the [Government of Nepal](Government_of_Nepal "Government of Nepal") handed over the management of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area to the Management Council.[[2]](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area#cite_note-aryal2010-2)

## Vegetation

The landscape of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area comprises cultivated lands, forests, pastures, rivers, high elevation lakes and [glaciers](Glacier "Glacier").[[1]](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area#cite_note-nbrb2007-1)

## Fauna

<Mammal> species include the [snow leopard](Snow_leopard "Snow leopard"), [Asian black bear](Asian_black_bear "Asian black bear"), and [red panda](Red_panda "Red panda"). Bird species symbolic of the area include the [golden-breasted fulvetta](Golden-breasted_fulvetta "Golden-breasted fulvetta"), [snow cock](Snow_cock "Snow cock"), [blood pheasant](Blood_pheasant "Blood pheasant"), and [red-billed chough](Red-billed_chough "Red-billed chough").[[1]](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area#cite_note-nbrb2007-1)

In April 2012, a [leopard cat](Leopard_cat "Leopard cat") was recorded by a [camera trap](Camera_trap "Camera trap") at an elevation of 4,474 m (14,678 ft). This record constitutes the highest known record to date. A [melanistic](Melanistic "Melanistic") [leopard](Indian_leopard "Indian leopard") was photographed at an elevation of 4,300 m (14,100 ft) in May 2012.[[3]](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area#cite_note-3) [Yellow-throated marten](Yellow-throated_marten "Yellow-throated marten") has been recorded up to 4,510 m (14,800 ft) elevation in alpine meadow.[[4]](Kanchenjunga_Conservation_Area#cite_note-4)

The **Qomolangma National Nature Preserve** (**QNNP**), also known as the **Chomolungma Nature Reserve** (**QNP**), is a [protected area](Protected_area "Protected area") 3.381 million hectares in size in the [Tibet Autonomous Region](Tibet_Autonomous_Region "Tibet Autonomous Region") of the [People’s Republic of China](People%E2%80%99s_Republic_of_China "People’s Republic of China"). Located on the [Roof of the World](Roof_of_the_World "Roof of the World") ("*Qomolangma*" is the [Tibetan](Tibetic_languages "Tibetic languages") name for [Mount Everest](Mount_Everest "Mount Everest")), the QNNP was one of the first nature preserves in the world to be administered and protected entirely by local volunteers. Through their continued efforts, significant achievements have been made in halting rampant [deforestation](Environmental_issues_in_China#Deforestation "Environmental issues in China"), unregulated tourism and [illegal hunting](Poaching "Poaching") of rare wildlife in the Qomolangma region. Active reforestation and garbage collection programs have also been undertaken to restore the environment.

The preserve, initially named Qomolangma Nature Preserve, was created on March 18, 1989 at the Tibet regional level. Support from then-Governor of Tibet, [Hu Jintao](Hu_Jintao "Hu Jintao"), was instrumental in shaping the community-based management design summarized below and also pushing through the landscape level size (in 1983, QNP was the largest nature reserve in Asia). In 1993, the [State Council of the People’s Republic of China](State_Council_of_the_People%E2%80%99s_Republic_of_China "State Council of the People’s Republic of China") elevated its protection to the national level and the QNP became QNNP.[[1]](Qomolangma_National_Nature_Preserve#cite_note-1)

## Physical Aspects

The QNNP contains along its border with <Nepal> four of the world's six highest mountains: <Everest>, <Lhotse>, <Makalu>, and [Cho Oyu](Cho_Oyu "Cho Oyu"). Also in this preserve is <Shishapangma>, 14th highest, the only [eight-thousander](Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander") meter peak totally in China. The preserve holds [Rongbuk Monastery](Rongbuk_Monastery "Rongbuk Monastery"), the highest monastery in the world at 4,500 meters and the highest agricultural fields in the world at 4,300 meters. In addition, the preserve has key pilgrimage sites for Tibetan Buddhism’s most famous poet saint, <Milarepa>.[[2]](Qomolangma_National_Nature_Preserve#cite_note-2)

The contiguous trans-border protected area that has become appended to the QNNP links with five protected areas in <Nepal>. These are [Makalu-Barun National Park](Makalu-Barun_National_Park "Makalu-Barun National Park"), [Sagarmatha National Park](Sagarmatha_National_Park "Sagarmatha National Park"), [Langtang National Park](Langtang_National_Park "Langtang National Park"), [Manaslu Conservation Area](Manaslu_Conservation_Area "Manaslu Conservation Area"), and [Annapurna Conservation Area](Annapurna_Conservation_Area "Annapurna Conservation Area") encompassing a total area of protected ecology greater than the land area of <Switzerland>—conserving multiple Himalayan ecosystems from very wet to very dry and from 1,000 feet of vertical elevation to 29,000 feet. Not adjacent by easy migratory distance away from the QNNP are significant protected areas in <Sikkim>, India, as well as the country of <Bhutan> which has over 40% of its land area protected.

## Management

QNNP is distinctive because no warden force protects its natural and cultural treasures. Management is by local communities, especially the governments of the four counties that comprise the preserve ([Tingri](Tingri_County "Tingri County"), Dinjie, Nyalam, Kyirong) with a Management Bureau in Shigatse, the prefecture headquarters. The four counties have a population estimated at over 90,000 people.[[3]](Qomolangma_National_Nature_Preserve#cite_note-autogenerated1-3) The official data sheet provided by the QNNP administration reports over 2,000 species of plants, 53 species of mammals, 206 species of birds, eight species of amphibians, 10 species of fish. ## Key Findings on Himalayan Transboundary Heritage Sites

While there are **no officially designated "transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Sites"** between India and Nepal or China-Nepal specifically in the Himalayas, there are significant transboundary protected area networks:

### 1. **Sacred Himalayan Landscape** 
A WWF-initiated transboundary conservation landscape spanning:
- **Nepal** (73%): Including Sagarmatha National Park, Makalu Barun National Park, Kanchenjunga Conservation Area
- **India** (24%): Including Khangchendzonga National Park, Singalila National Park, Neora Valley National Park, and various sanctuaries in Sikkim and West Bengal
- **Bhutan**: Torsa Strict Nature Reserve and Bhutan Biological Conservation Complex

This 39,021 km² landscape protects biodiversity corridors for species like snow leopards and red pandas across Nepal, India, and Bhutan.

### 2. **UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the Transboundary Network**

#### **Sagarmatha National Park (Nepal)** - UNESCO Natural World Heritage Site (1979)
- Includes Mount Everest (Sagarmatha)
- Shares border with Qomolangma National Nature Preserve in Tibet (China)
- Part of the Sacred Himalayan Landscape

#### **Khangchendzonga National Park (India/Sikkim)** - UNESCO Mixed World Heritage Site (2016)
- India's first "Mixed Heritage" site (cultural and natural criteria)
- Adjoins Kanchenjunga Conservation Area (Nepal) to the west
- Adjoins Qomolangma National Nature Preserve (Tibet/China) to the north
- Named after Kangchenjunga (third-highest mountain in the world at 8,586m)

### 3. **Qomolangma National Nature Preserve (China/Tibet)**
- 36,000 km² protected area on the China-Nepal border
- Contains Everest, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu, and Shishapangma
- Links with **5 protected areas in Nepal**: Makalu-Barun National Park, Sagarmatha National Park, Langtang National Park, Manaslu Conservation Area, and Annapurna Conservation Area
- Together these protected areas exceed the land area of Switzerland

### 4. **Kanchenjunga Conservation Area (Nepal)**
- Not a UNESCO site but part of transboundary landscape
- Established 1997
- Borders India's Khangchendzonga National Park to the east and China's Qomolangma NNP to the north

## Summary

The Himalayan region features an intricate network of transboundary protected areas, with **Khangchendzonga National Park** (India) and **Sagarmatha National Park** (Nepal) being the key UNESCO World Heritage Sites that form part of this cross-border conservation system spanning China (Tibet), Nepal, and India, with connections to Bhutan.

"Peace park" redirects here. For other uses, see [Peace park (disambiguation)](Peace_park_(disambiguation) "Peace park (disambiguation)").

A **transboundary protected area (TBPA)** is an ecological [protected area](Protected_area "Protected area") that spans boundaries of more than one [country](Country "Country") or sub-national entity. Such areas are also known as **transfrontier conservation areas (TFCAs)** or **peace parks**.[[1]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-1)[[2]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-:1-2)[[3]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-3)

TBPAs exist in many forms around the world,[[4]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-4) and are established for various reasons. The preservation of traditional animal migration patterns, ensuring sufficient food and water sources for population growth, is a critical reason for the creation of TBPAs. However, TBPAs also encourage [tourism](Tourism "Tourism"), economic development and goodwill between neighbouring countries, as well as making it easier for [indigenous](Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") inhabitants of the area to travel.[[5]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-5)

## Types of transboundary protected areas

TBPAs exist in various types of geographic configuration, with various levels of ecological protection, and with various levels of international cooperation. Additionally, different organizations employ different definitions for TBPAs. Julia Marton-Lefevre broadly defines TBPAs as "areas that involve a degree of cooperation across one or more boundaries between (or within) countries."[[6]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-:4-6) The Southern Africa Development Community's Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement defines Transfrontier Conservation Area as "the area or the component of a large ecological region that straddles the boundaries of two or more countries, encompassing one or more protected areas, as well as multiple resources use areas."[[7]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-7) The Global Transboundary Protected Areas Network (GTPAN) lists four types of "transboundary conservation areas:"

- Type 1: transboundary protected area;
- Type 2: transboundary conservation landscape and/or seascape;
- Type 3: transboundary conservation migration area; and
- Special designation: park for peace.[[8]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-:5-8)


GTPAN defines a transboundary protected area as "a clearly defined geographical space that includes protected areas that are ecologically connected across one or more international boundaries and involves some form of cooperation." **Terai Arc Landscape** (TAL) is composed of 14 [Indian](India "India") and [Nepalese](Nepal "Nepal") trans-border [protected ecosystems](Protected_area "Protected area") of the <Terai> ([Sanskrit](Sanskrit_language "Sanskrit language") for "lowlands") and nearby foothills of the <Himalayas>.[[1]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-missouri.edu-1)[[2]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-wwf-india-2) and encompassing 14 protected areas of Nepal and India. The area spans approximately 12.3 million acres (5 million hectares) and includes Nepal's [Bagmati River](Bagmati_River "Bagmati River") to the east and India's [Yamuna River](Yamuna_River "Yamuna River") to the west.[[1]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-missouri.edu-1) The TAL is home to many endangered mammals including the [Bengal tiger](Bengal_tiger "Bengal tiger") (of which it has one of the world's highest densities),[[1]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-missouri.edu-1)[[2]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-wwf-india-2) the [Indian rhinoceros](Indian_rhinoceros "Indian rhinoceros"), the [gaur](Gaur "Gaur"), the wild [Asian elephant](Asian_elephant "Asian elephant"), the [hispid hare](Hispid_hare "Hispid hare"), the [sloth bear](Sloth_bear "Sloth bear"), the [South Asian river dolphin](South_Asian_river_dolphin "South Asian river dolphin") and the [chital](Chital "Chital"), as well as over 500 species of birds, many endangered. Examples of birds are the endangered [Bengal florican](Bengal_florican "Bengal florican"), the [sarus crane](Sarus_crane "Sarus crane"), and the [black stork](Black_stork "Black stork").[[3]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-gov.np.terai-arc-3)

The rivers and wetlands of the TAL are rich and diverse [ecosystems](Ecosystem "Ecosystem") with many [endemic](Endemic "Endemic") species that support, besides birds and mammals, a wide range of fish, amphibians, and fresh water crustaceans.[[3]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-gov.np.terai-arc-3)

However, the area faces many challenges to the wildlife.[[4]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-wwfindia.org2-4) Of the 14 protected areas within the TAL, none is large enough, by itself, to sustain a population of tigers over time. If the protected areas were to be linked by wildlife corridors, individual tigers would be able to move from area to area, furthering its ability to survive long-term.[[1]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-missouri.edu-1)

TAL is densely populated and its welfare is of critical importance to its human and animal life.[[5]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-wwf-terai-nepal-5) Its approximately three million people are among the world's poorest (50% live below the poverty live) and generally subsist on the land.[[1]](Terai_Arc_Landscape#cite_note-missouri.edu-1)

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) designates [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") of outstanding universal value to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") which have been nominated by countries which are signatories to the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_India#cite_note-convention-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). The Terai Arc Landscape represents a significant conservation corridor, linking protected areas across both nations' borders and supporting biodiversity movement through the region.

Based on my comprehensive search through Wikipedia, I can provide you with the following findings about UNESCO World Heritage transboundary sites between India and Nepal:

## Key Findings

### **No Official UNESCO Transboundary World Heritage Sites**

According to the UNESCO World Heritage Sites by country data:
- **Nepal**: Has 4 World Heritage Sites but **0 officially designated shared/transboundary sites**
- **India**: Has 42 World Heritage Sites with **1 shared site** (but not with Nepal)

### **Protected Heritage Sites by Country**

**Nepal's UNESCO World Heritage Sites (4):**
1. Sagarmatha National Park (Natural) - 1979
2. Chitwan National Park (Natural) - 1984
3. Kathmandu Valley (Cultural) - 1979
4. Lumbini (Cultural) - 1997, birthplace of Buddha

**India's UNESCO World Heritage Sites (42):**
- 34 Cultural, 7 Natural, 1 Mixed (Khangchendzonga National Park)

### **Transboundary Conservation Areas (Not UNESCO World Heritage)**

While there are no officially designated **UNESCO World Heritage Site** transboundary properties between India and Nepal, there are significant **transboundary protected areas**:

#### **Terai Arc Landscape (TAL)**
- Composed of **14 trans-border protected ecosystems** of India and Nepal
- Covers approximately 5 million hectares
- Spans from Nepal's Bagmati River to India's Yamuna River
- Includes adjacent protected areas like:
  - **Chitwan National Park** (Nepal) - UNESCO World Heritage Site
  - **Valmiki National Park/Tiger Reserve** (India) - borders Chitwan National Park to the south

#### **Kangchenjunga Region**
- The mountain spans the Nepal-India border (three of five peaks directly on the border)
- **Khangchendzonga National Park** (India, Sikkim) - UNESCO World Heritage Site (Mixed) inscribed 2016
- However, this is **not** officially designated as a transboundary UNESCO site

### **Conclusion**

There are **no officially designated UNESCO World Heritage transboundary sites between India and Nepal**. However, the countries share several important **transboundary conservation landscapes** that work together for biodiversity preservation, particularly in the Terai Arc Landscape region. These protected areas function as connected ecosystems even without formal UNESCO transboundary designation.

Location of World Heritage Sites in Pakistan

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") are places of importance to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") as described in the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Pakistan#cite_note-convention-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.[[2]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Pakistan#cite_note-2) <Pakistan> ratified the convention on 23 July 1976, making its sites eligible for inclusion on the list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Pakistan#cite_note-Pakistan-3)

There are six World Heritage Sites in Pakistan, and a further 26 on the tentative list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Pakistan#cite_note-Pakistan-3) The first three sites were listed in 1980, the [Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro](Archaeological_Ruins_at_Moenjodaro "Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro"), [Buddhist Ruins of Takht-i-Bahi](Takht-i-Bahi "Takht-i-Bahi") and [Neighbouring City Remains at Sahr-i-Bahlol](Seri_Bahlol "Seri Bahlol"), and [Taxila](Taxila_(ancient) "Taxila (ancient)"). Two sites were listed in 1981 and the most recent site added to the list was the [Rohtas Fort](Rohtas_Fort "Rohtas Fort"), in 1997. All six sites are cultural.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Pakistan#cite_note-Pakistan-3)

## World Heritage Sites

UNESCO lists sites under [ten criteria](World_Heritage_Site#Selection_criteria "World Heritage Site"); each entry must meet at least one of the criteria. Criteria i through vi are cultural, and vii through x are natural.[[4]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Pakistan#cite_note-4)

Based on my comprehensive search through Wikipedia, I have found important information about UNESCO World Heritage transboundary sites between India and Pakistan.

## Key Finding: **There are NO UNESCO World Heritage transboundary sites shared between India and Pakistan**

### Pakistan's UNESCO World Heritage Sites
From the "World Heritage Sites by country" table:
- **Total sites**: 6 (all cultural)
- **Shared sites**: 0

Pakistan's 6 World Heritage Sites are:
1. Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro (1980)
2. Buddhist Ruins of Takht-i-Bahi and Neighbouring City Remains at Sahr-i-Bahlol (1980)
3. Taxila (1980)
4. Lahore Fort and Shalamar Gardens in Lahore (1981)
5. Makli Hill (1981)
6. Rohtas Fort (1997)

### India's UNESCO World Heritage Sites
India has significantly more World Heritage Sites (over 40, as of 2023), but **none are shared with Pakistan**.

### Why No Shared Sites?
The historical context explains this:
1. **Partition of 1947**: When India and Pakistan were partitioned, many historical sites were divided between the two countries, but none were designated as shared transboundary properties.
2. **Historic tensions**: The decades-long political tensions between India and Pakistan have made joint heritage nominations difficult.
3. **Different nomination strategies**: Each country has pursued its own separate nominations for UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

### Transboundary Sites in South Asia
While there are no India-Pakistan transboundary sites, there ARE other transboundary UNESCO World Heritage sites in South and Central Asia:
- **Silk Roads: The Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor** (China-Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan)
- **Western Tien-Shan** (Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan)
- **Sangha Trinational** (Cameroon-Central African Republic-Republic of Congo) in Africa

### Note on Biosphere Reserves
While there are no shared UNESCO World Heritage Sites, both countries participate in UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme, though not in joint transboundary biosphere reserves.

This contrasts with many other border regions in the world (like European countries) where transboundary World Heritage Sites are common and foster international cooperation on heritage preservation.

Location of World Heritage Sites in Bangladesh. Red dots are cultural sites, the green dot is a natural site.

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](UNESCO "UNESCO") (UNESCO) [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") are places of importance to [cultural](Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") or [natural heritage](Natural_heritage "Natural heritage") as described in the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, established in 1972.[[1]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-convention-1) Cultural heritage consists of monuments (such as architectural works, monumental sculptures, or inscriptions), groups of buildings, and sites (including archaeological sites). Natural features (consisting of physical and biological formations), geological and physiographical formations (including habitats of threatened species of animals and plants), and natural sites which are important from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty, are defined as natural heritage.[[2]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-2) <Bangladesh> accepted the convention on 3 August 1983, making its historical sites eligible for inclusion on the list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-Bangladesh-3)

As of 2022, there are three World Heritage Sites in Bangladesh, and a further five on the tentative list.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-Bangladesh-3) The first two sites listed were the [Mosque City of Bagerhat](Mosque_City_of_Bagerhat "Mosque City of Bagerhat") and the [Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur](Somapura_Mahavihara "Somapura Mahavihara"), in 1985. Both sites are cultural. The most recent site, the <Sundarbans>, was listed in 1997 and is a natural site.[[3]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-Bangladesh-3)

## World Heritage Sites

UNESCO lists sites under [ten criteria](World_Heritage_Site#Selection_criteria "World Heritage Site"); each entry must meet at least one of the criteria. Criteria i through vi are cultural, and vii through x are natural.[[4]](List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bangladesh#cite_note-4)

content:
Based on my Wikipedia research, I found that **The Sundarbans** is the primary UNESCO World Heritage transboundary site between India and Bangladesh. Here's a comprehensive summary:

## The Sundarbans - Transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Site

### **Key Facts:**

**Location & Governance:**
- **Spans across:** Ganges-Brahmaputra delta between Bangladesh and West Bengal, India
- **Governance:** Bangladesh controls 66%, India controls 34% of the area
- **Coordinates:** 21°43′59″N 88°52′08″E

### **Bangladesh Portion:**
- **Official UNESCO Name:** The Sundarbans
- **UNESCO Reference:** 798
- **Inscription Year:** 1997 (21st Session)
- **Area:** 139,500 hectares (539 sq mi)
- **Criteria:** Natural (ix)(x)
- **Includes:**
  - Sundarbans West Wildlife Sanctuary
  - Sundarbans South Sanctuary
  - Sundarbans East Sanctuary

### **India Portion:**
- **Official UNESCO Name:** Sundarbans National Park
- **UNESCO Reference:** 452
- **Inscription Year:** 1987 (11th Session)
- **Area:** 133,010 hectares (513.6 sq mi)
- **Criteria:** Natural (ix)(x)
- **Location:** South 24 Parganas, West Bengal
- **Additional Designations:** National Park, Tiger Reserve, Biosphere Reserve, and Ramsar Wetland (since 2019)

### **Significance:**
- **World's largest mangrove forest**
- **Critical habitat:** Largest reserve for Bengal tigers
- **Biodiversity:** Home to diverse bird, reptile, and invertebrate species, including salt-water crocodiles
- **Ecological importance:** Formed at the unified delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers on the Bay of Bengal

### **Additional UNESCO Designsations:**
- **Ramsar Wetland:** Designated in Bangladesh on May 21, 1992 (Reference no. 560) and India on January 30, 2019 (Reference no. 2370)

### **Context on Other World Heritage Sites:**
- **Bangladesh** has 3 total UNESCO World Heritage Sites:
  - Mosque City of Bagerhat (1985, Cultural)
  - Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur (1985, Cultural)
  - The Sundarbans (1997, Natural) - *This is the transboundary site*

- **India** has 42 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, with Sundarbans National Park being one of the natural sites

The Sundarbans represents an important example of transboundary natural heritage conservation, with both countries working to protect this ecologically critical mangrove ecosystem that supports endangered species and provides critical ecological services to the delta region.

A **transboundary protected area (TBPA)** is an ecological [protected area](Protected_area "Protected area") that spans boundaries of more than one [country](Country "Country") or sub-national entity. Such areas are also known as **transfrontier conservation areas (TFCAs)** or **peace parks**.[[1]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-1)[[2]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-:1-2)[[3]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-3)

TBPAs exist in many forms around the world,[[4]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-4) and are established for various reasons. The preservation of traditional animal migration patterns, ensuring sufficient food and water sources for population growth, is a critical reason for the creation of TBPAs. However, TBPAs also encourage [tourism](Tourism "Tourism"), economic development and goodwill between neighbouring countries, as well as making it easier for [indigenous](Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") inhabitants of the area to travel.[[5]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-5)

## Types of transboundary protected areas

TBPAs exist in various types of geographic configuration, with various levels of ecological protection, and with various levels of international cooperation. Additionally, different organizations employ different definitions for TBPAs. Julia Marton-Lefevre broadly defines TBPAs as "areas that involve a degree of cooperation across one or more boundaries between (or within) countries."[[6]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-:4-6) The Southern Africa Development Community's Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement defines Transfrontier Conservation Area as "the area or the component of a large ecological region that straddles the boundaries of two or more countries, encompassing one or more protected areas, as well as multiple resources use areas."[[7]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-7) The Global Transboundary Protected Areas Network (GTPAN) lists four types of "transboundary conservation areas:"

- Type 1: transboundary protected area;
- Type 2: transboundary conservation landscape and/or seascape;
- Type 3: transboundary conservation migration area; and
- Special designation: park for peace.[[8]](Transboundary_protected_area#cite_note-:5-8)


GTPAN defines a transboundary protected area as "a clearly defined geographical space that includes protected areas that are ecologically connected across one or more international boundaries and involves some form of cooperation." "World Heritage Site Manas National Park in Assam, India, to the south. It is listed as a tentative site in Bhutan's Tentative List for UNESCO inclusion."

This suggests that Royal Manas National Park is on Bhutan's tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage Site inclusion. Let me compile the comprehensive answer now based on all my research.

2. Bhutan currently has NO UNESCO World Heritage Sites inscribed

   - Manas National Park (India) - UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985
   - Royal Manas National Park (Bhutan) - borders Manas National Park and is on Bhutan's tentative list for UNESCO

content:
Based on my comprehensive search of Wikipedia, I can provide you with the following findings about UNESCO World Heritage transboundary sites between India and Bhutan:

## Main Finding: No Official UNESCO World Heritage Transboundary Sites

**There are currently NO official UNESCO World Heritage transboundary sites between India and Bhutan.** This is confirmed by multiple sources:

1. **Bhutan has no UNESCO World Heritage Sites inscribed** - According to the "World Heritage Sites by country" Wikipedia article, Bhutan is among the 29 countries that have "no properties inscribed on the World Heritage List"

2. **Bhutan's tentative sites** - While Bhutan has some sites on its tentative list for UNESCO inclusion (including Royal Manas National Park), none have been officially designated yet

## Important Transboundary Protected Area Relationship

However, there IS a significant transboundary protected area connection between the two countries:

### Manas National Park Complex

| Feature | Manas National Park (India) | Royal Manas National Park (Bhutan) |
|---------|----------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Location** | Chirang and Baksa District, Assam | Pemagatshel, Sarpang, Zhemgang, Bhutan |
| **UNESCO Status** | ✅ **World Heritage Site** (1985) | ⏳ Tentative List for UNESCO |
| **Area** | 500 km² (core area) | 1,057 km² |
| **Established** | 1990 (as National Park) | 1966 (Bhutan's oldest national park) |
| **IUCN Category** | II (National Park) | II (National Park) |
| **Additional Designations** | Biosphere Reserve, Project Tiger Reserve, Elephant Reserve | National Park |

### Key Points:

1. **Contiguous Protected Areas**: Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan is **contiguous** with Manas National Park in India, forming a continuous transboundary protected area across the India-Bhutan border.

2. **Shared Ecosystem**: Together, these parks protect exceptional biodiversity including rare and endangered species such as the Assam roofed turtle, hispid hare, golden langur, pygmy hog, and wild water buffalo.

3. **UNESCO Site on One Side Only**: Only the Indian side (Manas Wildlife Sanctuary) has been designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since December 1985. The Bhutan side (Royal Manas National Park) is listed on Bhutan's Tentative List for UNESCO inclusion.

4. **Biosphere Connection**: The Manas River forms the transboundary waterway between these protected areas, draining an area of 41,350 square kilometers across the border.

## Conclusion

While there is no officially designated transboundary UNESCO World Heritage Site between India and Bhutan, the **Manas-Royal Manas complex represents an important transboundary conservation area** with one side already UNESCO-inscribed and the other side on the tentative list. This demonstrates the ongoing conservation cooperation between the two neighboring countries in the Himalayan foothills.
